a Independent Researcher, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh 462020, India

Biomarker
Precision medicine
Therapeutics
ABSTRACT
Breast cancer is the most common cancer and the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Despite advancements in
detection and treatment, it remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths in women. Breast cancer stem cells
(BCSCs) are a crucial group of cells responsible for carcinogenesis, metastasis, medication resistance, and tumor
recurrence. Identifying and understanding their molecular pathways is essential for developing effective breast
cancer therapy. BCSCs are responsible for tumor genesis, development, metastasis, treatment resistance, and
recurrence. Biomarkers are essential tools for identifying high-risk patients, improving diagnostic accuracy,
developing follow-up programs, assessing treatment susceptibility, and predicting prognostic outcomes. Stem cell
intervention therapy can provide specialized tools for precision therapy. Biomarker analysis in cancer patients is
crucial to identify cells associated with disease progression and post-therapeutic relapse. However, negative posttherapeutic impacts can enhance cancer stemness by boosting BCSCs plasticity phenotypes, activating stemness
pathways in non-BCSCs, and promoting senescence escape, leading to tumor relapse and metastasis. Despite the
advancements in precision medicine, challenges persist in identifying stem cell markers, limiting the number of
eligible patients for treatment. The diversity of biomedical research hinders the development of
individualization-based preventative, monitoring, and treatment strategies, especially in oncology. Integrating
and interpreting clinical and scientific data remains challenging. The development of stem cell-related indicators
could significantly improve disease precision, enabling stem cell-targeted therapy and personalized treatment
plans, although BCSCs are promising for breast cancer treatment optimization, serving as biomarkers for current
therapy modalities. This summary discusses recent advancements in breast cancer stem cell research, including
biomarkers, identification methods, molecular mechanisms, and tools for studying their biological origin and
lineage development for precision medicine.
1. Introduction
Breast cancer (BC) is a significant cause of cancer-related mortality
for women globally, with metastasis being a major cause of death [1].
Breast cancer accounts for 12.5 % of all new annual cancer cases
worldwide, making it the most common cancer in the world. BC is a
heterogeneous disease with varying treatment responses and diseasespecific outcomes due to its wide range of subtypes and stages. Breast
cancer, often linked to women, can also affect men, with male breast
cancer accounting for about 1 % of all breast cancers, despite its lesser
frequency compared to women. There are different types of female
breast cancer including invasive ductal carcinoma, invasive lobular
carcinoma, inflammatory breast cancer, Paget’s disease of the breast,
angiosarcoma of the breast, phyllodes tumors, ductal carcinoma in situ
(DCIS), lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), HER2 status, triple-negative
breast cancer (TNBC) metastatic breast cancer etc. Gene expression
profiling and immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be used to identify
different subtypes of BC, such as TNBC, which is characterized by the
absence of ER, PR, and HER2, and ER-positive, HER2-positive, and
progesterone-positive BC (PR-PR) [2]. TNBC accounts for approximately
15 % of all BC cases among the three immune-histochemical subtypes
and is most closely linked to poor prognosis and reduced survival rate
due to early organ metastases and a lack of clinically proven targeted
therapy [3]. The basal-like subtype of breast cancer, comprising 80 % of
breast cancer stem cells (BSCSs), is the most aggressive molecular subtype [4]. Breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) contribute to the aggressive
progression and recurrence of the disease by self-renewal and tumor
initiation.

(TICs) [5], are the primary cause of BC tumor growth, metastasis, and

aggressive, diverse, and treatment-resistant malignancies. The makeup
of tumor cell subpopulations varies with treatment regimens like
chemotherapy or radiation. Breast cancer treatment varies across
countries, with access to surgery and radiation therapy being crucial for
improving outcomes. Survivors often face pain, fatigue, sexual
dysfunction, dermatology concerns, cardiovascular issues, and low bone
density due to their cancer treatment. Recent advancements in targeting
BCSCs have shown promise in increasing remission rates, but targeted
therapy remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity.
Tumor cells with a high potential for proliferation are first identified
and eliminated, while cancer stem cells (CSCs) continue to live. A small
percentage of tumor cells undergo therapy-induced senescence (TIS),
which can alter the tumor microenvironment and have tumorpromoting effects. CSCs can result in tumor relapses and are resistant
to treatment [6]. CSCs are present in breast cancer, with studies showing
that xeno-transplanted cell subpopulations enriched for CSCs can produce tumors from a small fraction of unselected cells [7].
The CSC hypothesis suggests that cancer recurrence and metastasis
are caused by this particular subpopulation of cells, as they are the only
ones capable of forming tumors. Isolating candidate CSCs is essential to
showcasing their functional traits, which has been made possible by the
application of cell-surface markers and labeling of cells that display
stemness-related traits. The discovery of CSCs in 1994 was made
possible through various studies, including the identification of a small
subset of cells proliferating slower than the mature blast cells [4]. These
CSCs have distinct surface markers, which can be separated using
fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) or other immunoselection
techniques [4]. Flow cytometry was used to concentrate CD44 + CD24-/
low cells, which were then transplanted into NOD/SCID mice after
nonepithelial cells were eliminated. In NOD/SCID animals, the CD44 +
CD24-/low cells formed tumors from fewer cells than the mixed population, which was 10- to 50-fold more abundant in these cells [8,9]. The
generated xenografts shared the same phenotypic variety as the initial
tumors. Cell subpopulations with high aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)
activity were shown to be enriched for CSCs using a similar experimental
paradigm[10]. The ALDEFLUOR test enables flow cytometry to enrich
for these cells [10]. Aldehyde dehydrogenase family 1 member A1
(ALDH1A1) in 481 primary breast carcinomas showed its independent
prognostic relevance. However, it has been questioned which aldehyde
dehydrogenase isoform(s) in malignant breast epithelial cells is
responsible for ALDEFLUOR-positivity. Pece and his colleagues (2010)
extracted enough normal mammary stem cells to generate a signature of
gene expression by taking advantage of their quiescent state [11]. The
grade of breast tumors correlated with the ensuing gene signature, and
the CSC content of breast tumors determined their grade. Alpha-6
integrin, also known as CD49f, was a prominent indication of the
normal mammary stem cell-derived signature (ITGA6) [12]. While CSC
markers in primary breast tumors have been the subject of multiple
research, their exact clinical importance is still unknown and their
conclusions have varied.
Cancer is a complex and heterogeneous disease, with treatment
failures and individual differences in effectiveness affecting overall
survival rates. This highlights the need for personalized, targeted anticancer treatments to overcome these challenges. precision medicine
involves measuring key tumor characteristics to determine the best
therapeutic plan for each patient, effectively treating their cancer and
preventing relapse [13,14]. The use of novel molecular analysis in
cancer research has led to extensive data gathering. This article examines recent developments in precision medicine for BC, a frequent and
fatal disease, focusing on the function of stem cells and BCSCs in this
regard. This review also covers the present understanding of BCSC
biomarkers, their relative abundance, and clinical significance in BC,
techniques for BCSC identification and isolation, the mechanism controlling BCSCs and their potential for therapeutics, regarding the origins
of BCSCs, and approaches for investigating BCSC lineage in precision
oncology. This review article covers recent progress in breast cancer
stem cell research, focusing on biomarkers, identification techniques,
molecular mechanisms, and tools for understanding their biological
genesis and lineage development in the context of precision medicine.
2. Origin of BCSCs
The origin of tumors can be influenced by various factors, including
the type of tumor, the type of stem cells, and the type of cell type [15].
Tissue-resident stem cells or their offspring may be the primary source of
tumor start, which can occur during tissue regeneration, response to
toxins, radiation, infections, or metabolic factors that result in mutations
[5]. Tumor suppressors are inactivated, and oncogenes are overexpressed during the transformation process, allowing cells to proliferate
out of control [16]. Tissue-resident stem cells have an infinite capacity
for expansion, making them a potential source of tumors. Lineage
tracing is a commonly employed method to monitor the movement,
reproduction, and specialization of particular cells. Lineage tracing involves identifying all descendants of a single cell. Traditional single-cell
lineage tracing assays have been the gold standard for determining the
origin of a tumor. Still, this approach has limitations due to its reliance
on a few markers [15]. The field of studying BCSC genesis has expanded
with the advent of single-cell transcriptomics and single-cell genetic
lineage tracing. The main theories about the development of BCSCs are
the progenitor cells’ mutation-induced pluripotency into cancer stem
cells (Fig. 1), the dedifferentiation of adult mammary cells into stem
cells through the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and the generation of BCSCs from normal stem cells [4,17].
The hierarchical or CSC model assumes that only a tiny percentage of
stem/progenitor cells within a tumor can replicate the tumor and reinforce the tumor hierarchy. In the linear hierarchy model of CSC creation,
cancer is driven by transformation events in a stem or progenitor cell,
leading to the development of more differentiated progeny as the tumor
progresses. The offspring with distinct characteristics have a decreased
ability to grow tumors. BCSCs have characteristics similar to minimally
differentiated progenitor cells, including self-renewal, proliferation, and
differentiation [4,18]. Research also indicates that differentiated
mammary cells may become CSCs when exposed to harmful environmental factors like radiation and chemotherapy [19]. This hypothesis,
known as clonal evolution or the stochastic model, postulates that all
tumor cells have a comparable capacity to cause tumors and that
intratumoral clonal evolution, caused by a series of mutations, results in
tumor heterogeneity [20]. Cell stem cells in solid malignancies have a
unidirectional hierarchy, meaning only the CSC population may prevent
a tumor from growing. The clonal evolution model suggests that
genetically unstable cells accumulate genomic and genetic alterations
over time, leading to increased tumor aggressiveness, resistance, and
heterogeneity [21]. The cellular plasticity model postulates that various
cellular states can interconvert, explaining why these models are not
mutually exclusive [22].
The lineage tracing test in mice models is currently the gold standard
for defining the origin of BCSCs, enabling tracking of an animal singlecell clone by labeling different cell subpopulations with different cellspecific promotors [4]. The most popular method for monitoring the
migration, division, and proliferation of certain cells in vivo is lineage
tracing. From a molecular and cellular biology standpoint, lineage
tracing has broadened the platforms accessible for drug screening, cell
plasticity research, disease model building, and the development of
customized medicine. Lineage tracing offers fresh perspectives on the
growth and regeneration of digestive organs as well as methods for
identifying the etiology and course of digestive diseases.
However, recent developments in single-cell RNA sequencing
(scRNA-seq) have enabled the objective characterization of molecular
states and cell identities in heterogeneous tissues at an unprecedented
resolution [23]. Studies have shown that mature luminal subpopulation
are downstream of less differentiated luminal progenitor cells in TNBC

3. Methods for the identification and isolation of breast cancer
stem cells
Four primary methods are used for identifying and isolating BCSCs
are based on their functional characteristics or high expression of cell
surface markers [4]. A popular technique is based on specific cell surface
indicators or combinations of biomarkers, which is a top focus in cancer
research (Table 1). Other techniques, such as mammosphere formation,
ALDEFLUOR assay, and side population cell isolation using Hoechst
33342, are based on intrinsic properties of CSCs, such as high expression
of ALDH1, ATP-binding cassette transporters, and CSC self-renewal and
proliferation [4].
4. Therapy-induced senescence: its hallmarks, biomarkers, and
its role in BCSC generation
Senescence is a process in cancer cells that occurs when exposed to
DNA damage agents like radiation and chemotherapy [30,31]. This
process, known as tumor suppressor senescence (TIS), has been extensively studied due to its significant impact on patients’ long-term outcomes. TIS is initiated and maintained by activating one or more tumor
suppressor pathways, such as p53, p16 (Ink4a), p21 (Waf1), and retinoblastoma (RB) [5]. Cancer cells deficient in functional p53 and RB
protein can still cause the senescence phenotype. Senescence and TIS
have negative effects on treatment outcomes and prognoses, but they
also attract immune cells, cause inflammation, and eliminate senescent
tumor cells [5]. However, senescence can enhance CSC development by
playing a significant pro-tumorigenic role. Classical biomarkers of
cellular senescence include senescence-associated beta-galactosidase
(SA-ß-gal) activity, p53 protein expression, nuclear p53 concentration,
p14 (Arf), p16 (Ink4a), and p21 (Waf1) upregulation, SASP, and
frequently senescence-associated heterochromatic foci (SAHF) [5].
Senescent cells also exhibit levels of heterochromatin protein 1
(HP1) gamma, histone H3 di- or tri-methylated lysine 9 (H3K9Me2/3),
and histone H2A variant (macroH2A) [32]. To accurately evaluate the
pathological fate of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), it is
necessary to verify the concurrent expression of several markers associated with the p53 pathway [33]. In cancers, innate and adaptive immune cells form a ‘senescence surveillance’ mechanism when induced,
preventing premalignant cells from undergoing cancer growth [31,34].
More research is needed to demonstrate the significance of the chemokine axis in initiation and maintenance of senescence and ensure
adequate immune surveillance.
Breast cancer stem cells, have been identified through various biomarkers (Table 2) found in tumor samples, animal models, and cell lines
since their discovery in 2003 [4]. These biomarkers reveal several
subgroups and variance among BC subtypes, which correlates with
clinical outcomes and therapy responses. Al-Hajj and his colleagues
(2003) were the first to use cell surface markers CD44 and CD24 to
detect tumor-initiating CSCs in BC [35]. Recent studies have used other
markers, such as ABCG2, CD133, CD49f, LGR5, SSEA-3, CD70, and
PROCR, to characterize BCSCs. CD44, CD24, and ALDH1 are the most
widely used biomarkers for identifying BCSC characteristics [4,36,37].
Research has shown that drug resistance, metastasis, tumor initiation,
and progression are caused by BCSCs with the CD44+/CD24� /low
phenotype and ALDH1+ [38]. Other less commonly used biomarkers for
BCSC detection include CD90, PCOR, CD61, CD133, and CD49f. Overexpression of CD133 is linked to poor prognosis in invasive BC [39].

Signaling pathways such as Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, and Hippo play a
crucial role in regulating the self-renewal of BCSCs. The Notch signaling
pathway is a crucial signaling cascade involved in the preservation of the
BCSC phenotype [43]. It is essential for self-renewal, stem cell maintenance, and cellular differentiation during the developmental stage of
cells. Notch signaling controls stem cell proliferation and differentiation
into luminal progenitor cells in the mouse mammary gland. In the
xenograft model, γ-secretase inhibition prevented the development of
the active Notch intracellular domain (NCID), thereby stopping tumor
growth [44] and decreasing the populations of CD44+/CD24� /low and
ALDH + BCSCs. Overexpression of the Notch ligand DLL1 leads to
increased Notch signaling, which in turn stimulates angiogenesis,
migration, proliferation, and the CSC phenotype [45]. The abbrent Wnt/
β-catenin signaling system supports the renewal, proliferation, and differentiation of BCSC. Wnt/β-catenin signaling is one of the most
important mechanisms controlling stem cell division and self-renewal
[46,47]. Oncogenic stimulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases
the development of human mammospheres and enriches mammary stem
and progenitor cells. Wnt signaling contributes to BC chemoresistance
and radioresistance, but blocking Wnt/β-catenin signaling inhibits the
CSC-like phenotype, which reduces breast cancer metastasis [48].
The Canonical Wnt signaling pathway, which relies on β-Catenin and
T cell factor (TCF)/lymphoid enhancer factor (LEF), primarily regulates
breast cancer cell proliferation and the maintenance of ’stemness’.
Notch signaling regulates the differentiation of breast epithelial cells in
the course of normal development. Different studies have shown that the
Notch system significantly contributes to the advancement of breast
cancer by involving the overexpression and/or aberrant genetic
expression of notch receptors and ligands, which regulate angiogenesis.
Hypoxia-induced up-regulation of Notch ligands led to the activation of
Notch signaling. HIF-2α facilitated the transformation of stem cell
characteristics by stimulating Notch and Wnt pathways in breast cancer
cells.
HIF-2α overexpression can trigger both Wnt and Notch signaling,
which in turn supports the stem cell phenotype, treatment resistance,
and overexpression of BCSC markers [49]. The hedgehog (Hh) pathway
is a major regulator of cell fate and plays a significant role in cellular
activities during embryonic development [50]. Proliferation, migration,
metastasis, and aggressiveness of BC have all been linked to overexpression of the major Hh pathway regulators, SHH, DHH, PTCH1, and
GLI1. The Hh/GLI signalling pathway involves ligands (Shh, Ihh, and
Dhh), transmembrane receptors (Ptch1 and Ptch2), transcription factors
(GLI1-3), and signalling regulators that collaborate to either inhibit or
stimulate (Shh, Ihh, Dhh, SMO, GLI1-3) the signalling process. Hippo

The Hippo pathway, crucial for organogenesis and regeneration
[51], is another significant circuit involving CSCs. It consists of a core
transcriptional module and a core regulatory kinase module. The Hippo
pathway is crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis by balancing
proliferation and differentiation. The pathway functions via a series of
kinases that ultimately activate the Yes-associated protein (YAP) and its
paralog, the transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ).
TAZ is a transcriptional regulator that is often activated in human cancers. Recent studies show that TAZ is crucial for the development or
progression of the majority of solid tumours. Their activation triggers
the characteristics of cancer stem cells, including proliferation, resistance to chemotherapy, and the spread of cancer to other parts of the
body. TAZ expression is significantly higher in tumors generated from
BCSCs than in tumors not derived from BCSCs [52]. The BCSC pool’s
upkeep has been linked to the interaction between TAZ and the extracellular matrix. Treatment with Dasatinib, a multi-target kinase inhibitor, demonstrated the ability to destroy the CSC population selectively
[53]. Dasatinib belongs to a category of drugs known as kinase inhibitors. It functions by inhibiting the activity of an aberrant protein that
stimulates cancer cells to proliferate. This inhibits the proliferation of
cancer cells. Dasatinib enhances the sensitivity of KRAS-mutant cancer
cells to mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase inhibitor via inhibiting
TAZ activity.
6. BCSC subpopulations and role of non-coding RNAs in BCSCs
Research has identified nonoverlapping cell groups in primary
human breast tumors using CD44+/CD24� /low and ALDH1 biomarkers
[4]. BCSCs with the ALDH1 + phenotype exhibit an epithelial and
proliferative phenotype, similar to luminal stem cells, while those with
CD44+/CD24� /low markers exhibit a mesenchymal and quiescent
phenotype similar to basal stem cells [4]. BCSCs can revert between
mesenchymal and epithelial states during EMT, under cytokine
signaling control. Both BCSC populations shared the ability to replicate a
tumor in a xenograft model. However, neither ALDH1 + BCSCs nor
CD44+/CD24� /low BCSCs exhibit 100 % sphere forming capability in
vitro [4]. The most tumorigenic and metastatic activity is exhibited by
tiny populations of BCSCs that simultaneously express both ALDH1 +
and CD44+/CD24� /low biomarkers, capable of forming tumors [4,54].
Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) have many functions in essential biological processes including as transcription, genomic imprinting, chromatin remodelling, and epigenetics, acting in a specific locationdependent manner. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) and long noncoding RNAs
(lncRNAs) are two primary groups of non-protein-coding transcripts.
Non-coding RNAs play a role in regulating communication inside and
between cells in breast cancer. Non-coding RNAs regulate intracellular
signalling to influence several physiological processes such as the levels
and function of oestrogen receptor α (ERα), cell proliferation, invasion,
migration, apoptosis, and stem cell characteristics. Evidence is accumulating that ncRNAs are dysregulated in breast cancer and BCSCs.

Some miRNAs have an oncogenic role, increasing drug resistance and
promoting BCSC characteristics. Other miRNAs function as tumor suppressors, reducing BCSC stemness or reverse treatment resistance when
overexpressed. These miRNAs regulate BCSC self-renewal, tumor
metastasis, and treatment resistance through various pathways. Some
miRNAs, such as Let-7, miR-146, miR-142, miR-374, miR-600, and miR340, regulate the Wnt signaling pathway and the BCSC phenotype [4].
Long intergenic non-coding RNAs (LincRNAs) can finely adjust the
expression of nearby genes with unique tissue specificity through
various means, showcasing our developing knowledge of the non-coding
genome. LincRNAs, which are longer than 200 nucleotides and do not
code for proteins, can interact with miRNAs to affect the stability of
mRNAs or attract transcription factors to control gene expression [56].
Recent research has shown the involvement of lincRNAs, HOTAIR, ROR,
and 00,617 in BCSCs via the control of EMT signaling pathways [57].
LincRNAs [58], such as NRAD1, NEAT1, H19, FGF13-AS1, SOX2OT,
MALAT-1, and ES1, are related to BC stemness through various processes. These ncRNAs serve as biomarkers and therapeutic targets for
BCSC-directed therapies and shed light on the regulatory mechanisms
underlying stemness.
7. Relative BCSCs abundance in different breast cancer subtypes
and their clinical relevance
Breast cancer subtypes have varying proportions of CD44+/CD24� /
low BCSC subpopulations, with basal-like tumors having larger proportions than luminal type tumors [54]. The CD44+/CD24� /low
phenotype is enriched in basal/mesenchymal BC cell lines, while the
CD44� /low/CD24 + cell population is enriched in luminal cell lines. A
current research indicates that individuals with TNBC and metastatic BC
who exhibit the CD44+/CD24� /low phenotype have a poor prognosis
[59]. However, inconsistent findings may be due to using various BC
subtypes in separate studies or distinct patient cohorts.
Studies have shown that varying expressions of CD44/CD24 and
ALDH1 in distinct subtypes of breast cancer. The CD44+/CD24� /low
phenotype is predominantly found in basal-like breast cancers, whereas
ALDH1 + cells are more prevalent in HER2-overexpression (HER2-OE)
and basal/epithelial breast cancers. A subgroup of BCSCs is identified by
elevated expression of ALDH1, which is correlated with a poor prognosis

8. New targeted approaches and therapeutic drugs targeting
BCSC subpopulations
Two hypotheses explain how BCSCs become multidrug resistance
(MDR) in BC that show elevated resistance to standard chemotherapy
treatments [5]. The first hypothesis suggests that only BCSCs expressing
ATP-binding cassette transporters (ABC transporters) can repopulate the
tumor by asymmetrical cell division following exposure to anticancer
drugs. The second hypothesis suggests that only BCSCs survive chemotherapy and evolve new, more aggressive cell morphologies due to
accumulated mutations [5]. Research on CSCs has been a topic of interest, with some strategies combining CSC-targeted treatments with
traditional non-targeted therapies (Table 3). Kinase inhibitors and
targeting Wnt and β-catenin pathways are two strategies for CSCtargeted treatments, some of which have reached clinical stage
[47,62]. Immunological strategies targeting CSCs by MHC-restricted
death include vaccination, antibody-based strategies, checkpoint inhibitor targeting, and adoptive cell transfer. MHC-unrestricted killing
can occur through chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell methods,
which are currently used when first-line medicines fail. CAR T-cellbased therapies have advanced into solid malignancies [63] due to their
promising outcomes in hematological disorders. CAR T-cells are Tlymphocytes that have been genetically modified to target a specific
antigen without being constrained by HLA, combining the specificity of
antibodies with the activity of T-cells.

ALDH + phenotype in patient biopsy samples [64,65]. Two monoclonal
antibodies, vantictumab (OMP-18R5) and cirtuzumab (UC-961), have
been investigated for metastatic breast cancer [4]. LGK-974, an inhibitor
of the endogenous Wnt palmitoleoylase Porcupine (PORCN), has been

The rising evidence that CSCs contribute to cancer development and
recurrence suggests that developing anti-CSC medicines will likely
enhance cancer patients’ long-term survival rates. A proof of principle
for targeting CSCs was demonstrated in Acute myeloid leukemia (AML, a
type of cancer that starts in the blood-forming cells of the bone marrow),
where the anti-leukemia medication TDZD-8 selectively destroyed
leukaemia stem cells while not impacting normal hematopoietic stem
and progenitor cells [67]. Many of the mechanisms now being investigated as possible therapeutic targets in CSCs have been proven to govern
normal stem and progenitor cells, thus identifying techniques to selectively target the pathways in cancer including breast cancer will be
crucial. Recent research has focused on Notch and Wnt pathways as
regulators of cell destiny in the breast [68-71]. It’s not surprising that
they could be therapeutic targets in CSCs. In a model of Notch1-driven
mammary carcinogenesis, inhibiting Notch signaling caused tumor
regression and decreased tumorsphere development in vitro [72]. In
response to hypoxia, the Notch ligand Jagged2 was upregulated in
breast cancer cells and bone marrow derived cells, resulting in CSC
growth [73]. Notch 4 activity is increased in breast CSCs, and Notch and
Wnt signaling were found to mediate radio-resistance in breast progenitor and CSCs [74-76]. Pygo2, a Wnt co-activator, augmented
mammosphere formation in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells [77]. In
contrast, pygo2 deletion in MMTV-Wnt1 tumor cells reduced both
mammosphere and tumor-forming capability [78].
The discovery of Salinomycin in a screen for CSC inhibitors highlighted the potential therapeutic value of targeting Wnt signaling. Salinomycin selectively eliminates CSCs by blocking Wnt signaling and
triggering apoptosis [79-81]. Salinomycin also destroyed iCSCL-10A
cells resistant to Taxol and Actinomycin D [82]. Metformin, an antidiabetic medicine, also appears to be effective against CSCs. Metformin targets CSC and can work together with chemotherapeutic medications to lower CSC levels and tumor progression [83,84]. Metformin
inhibits NF-κB nuclear translocation and STAT3 phosphorylation in
CSCs, relative to non-CSCs (Hirsch et al., 2013). Metformin may be
effective for treating TAM-resistant ER + malignancies that upregulate
NF-κB [85]. Metformin therapy successfully overcome Herceptin™
resistance in a Her2-positive xenograft model [86]. A list of natural
product and synthetic pharmaceuticals targeting BCSCs are shown in the
Table 4. Cell surface receptors are appealing therapeutic targets because
they are drug-accessible. PDGFR-β, a growth factor receptor, was found
to be downstream of FOXC2 in cells undergoing EMT. Both proteins
were expressed in CSC-enriched populations of SUM159 and HMLER
cells [87]. Sunitinib, a PDGFR-β inhibitor, inhibited tumor development
and metastasis in FOXC2-expressing tumor cells [87]. Thus, sunitinib
may be useful in the treatment of CSC caused by EMT. FGF-receptor 2
(FGFR2) was found in CSC recovered from a MMTV-PyMT mice breast
cancer model [88]. Furthermore, FGFR2-expressing human tumor cells
were more tumorigenic than FGFR2-negative cells in the xenograft
studies. TKI258, a FGFR inhibitor, lowered the number of CSCs in
MMTV-PyMT-driven tumors while delaying tumor progression [88].
Expansion may impede tumor development and allow for more
effective CSC eradication. Cicalese and his colleagues (2009) found that
restoring p53 function in Her2 over-expressing cells resulted in asymmetric cell division in CSCs and reduced tumor formation [89].
Hedgehog (Hh) signaling via Bmi1 enhanced the frequency of mammosphere forming cells, which was reversed using the Hh inhibitor
cyclopamine [90]. Piggott and his colleagues (2011) found that suppressing cFLIP decreased CSCs in response to TRAIL, resulting in fewer
initial tumors and nearly no metastases in transplant mice [91]. cFLIP
suppression also lowered MFU enrichment post mammosphere transit,
implying that symmetric CSC division was disrupted. To avoid CSC
creation from non-CSCs, it’s important to address the plasticity of tumor
cells. Meyer and his group (2009) found that inhibiting Activin/Nodal
signaling prevented CD44 + CD24+ (non-stem) cells from producing
CD44 + CD24low (CSC) offspring [92]. Therapeutic ablation of certain
cell types may only provide temporary relief from tumor development.
To effectively treat cancer, it’s important to target both CSCs and nonCSCs, as some medicines may promote CSC formation. Repertaxin, a
CXCR1 inhibitor, increased Fas expression in tumor cells and inhibited
IL-8 signaling via CXCR1 to destroy CSCs [93]. Combining GCV with
TMZ to target both CSCs and non-CSCs considerably reduces tumor
burden compared to GCV treatment alone [94]. The scientists were
unable to determine the impact of suppressing the TK transgene on
overall survival due to cell outgrowth. Current cancer medicines are
approved only for their ability to reduce tumor size, without considering
their impact on CSCs. As a result, in addition to creating medications
that target CSCs, new assays will be required to detect changes in CSC
function that, on their own, may not result in a reduction in tumor size.
The efficacy of CSC-targeted treatments could also be measured by
analyzing cancer recurrence in patients treated with combination
medication regimens.
9. Role of BCSCs, as biomarkers for BC precision medicine
Precision medicine is a strategy to the treatment of disease while
considering inconsistencies in the genes, environment, and lifestyle of
each person [95-97]. The goal of recent advancements in omics technologies has been to provide increased accuracy in precision medicine.
The foundation of the precision-medicine strategy is the identification of
appropriate biomarkers to forecast the effectiveness of tailored therapy
in a particular patient population. Certain druggable mutations have
been found in breast cancer.
Clinical trials focusing on metastatic cancer patients are exploring
new treatment approaches, particularly for BCSCs. CSCs have been
isolated from various cancer types using dye-efflux sub-population
isolation techniques or cell surface marker molecules. Their role as
predictors of poor prognosis and therapeutic targets is growing, with
studies showing that tumors with higher levels of CD44 and CD133 have

10. Conclusions and future perspectives
The study examines the expression of potential CSC markers in primary breast carcinomas, finding that all markers had a high correlation
with negative ER status. Additional markers are needed for IHC quantification of CSCs in ER + tumors, which account for 75-80 % of all
breast cancers. The most potent predictor of outcome in ER-disease was
a composite score representing the expression of all four markers,
although only ITGA6 maintained independent prognostic relevance.
Research BCSCs has made substantial progress in understanding their
role in tumor development, spread, metastasis, medication resistance,
and recurrence. Current therapies target BCSC signaling pathways and
factors that preserve BCSC features, but their exact origins remain unknown. Recent advancements in single-cell genetic/epigenetic lineage
tracing, single-cell transcriptomics technology, and computational algorithms for lineage reconstruction and differentiation trajectories
could lead to the identification of the origin of BCSCs. Targeted therapies for BCSCs have been developed, with post-therapeutic local biopsies
being particularly beneficial for identifying therapeutically targetable
targets in residual tumor tissue and assessing the likelihood of tumor
relapse based on multivariate biomarkers. Targeted therapies, such as
immunotherapies, CAR NK, and CAR T cells, can be part of this secondary specific therapy.
A potential strategy to reduce the off-target effects of chemotherapy
drugs and improve patient outcomes in the clinic is precision medicine.
This is an essential method for treating breast cancer successfully. In
order to anticipate the effectiveness of targeted therapy in particular
patient groups, precision medicine necessitates the selection of appropriate biomarkers. Numerous potentially druggable mutations in breast
tumours have been found, which could be used to build new therapies
for breast cancer patients. Developments in omics technologies have
concentrated on the more precise tactics of precision therapy. The
advancement of next-generation sequencing technologies has stoked
expectations for breast cancer treatment plans based on precision
medicine. Additionally, focusing on BCSCs and signalling pathways may
be a useful strategy for treating breast cancer. When combined with
suitable single modalities, combination therapy techniques have the
potential to greatly enhance the precision medicine treatment of metastatic BC. It has been difficult to create predictive BCSC biomarker
markers, nevertheless, and more research is required. Patients’ chances
of survival will increase with the advancement and application of nextgeneration sequencing technology as well as additional clinical studies
including precision medicine-based treatments for breast cancer. The
use of BCSCs in metastatic breast cancer therapy could be revolutionised
by precision-medicine techniques. The field of precision medicine for
life-saving breast cancer therapy must be advanced by coordinated efforts by researchers, medical professionals, and regulatory agencies.
